Let's dive into Chapter 3: Choosing to Live—The Rejection of Suicide.
Once you really see the absurd for what it is, and you stop reaching for all the usual escapes, you’re left with a big, uncomfortable question. If life doesn’t have some grand, ultimate meaning, then why keep going? Why not just call it quits?
Now, that might sound harsh, but it’s not about despair. It’s about logic. If nothing matters, what’s the point in continuing?
For a lot of people, suicide is simply unthinkable. It’s seen as something only the desperate or the deeply troubled consider—a last resort, or even a weakness. But when you approach it as a philosophical question, things get a lot more complicated. It’s not really about pain, or even suffering—it’s about this question: is life worth living, in a world that doesn’t hand us a ready-made purpose?
Maybe you’ve had a moment where you felt totally adrift. Every day felt pointless, empty—a kind of gray nothingness. And in that space, the idea of ending it all might have popped into your head. Not out of sadness, but from this sense that, well, nothing really matters. In that moment, suicide stops being some abstract concept and becomes a very real possibility—not a threat, but an option on the table.
But the thing about seeing the absurd is, it opens up another path. If life has no deep, cosmic meaning, then it’s up to us to make our own. Just living, in spite of all that, becomes an act of rebellion. To wake up each day and keep going, even when everything feels meaningless—that’s how you claim your own freedom and dignity.
Suicide, when you look at it this way, isn’t really a solution—it’s more like surrender. It’s a way of trying to escape the absurd, of saying, “I can’t handle this.” It’s admitting that the lack of meaning is just too much. But choosing to live, to keep pushing forward despite everything, is a way of owning the absurd and making it part of your story.
And you know, there’s a kind of heroism in that choice. Not the dramatic, movie-style heroics, but the everyday kind. The quiet courage it takes to get up, face the world as it is, and keep going. It’s in finding joy in little things, in creating your own meaning out of thin air, in loving and hoping and laughing—even if you can’t always explain why.
Think about a teacher, just grinding through the same routine day after day. Maybe life feels dull, even pointless at times. But then, there’s a student’s smile, or the satisfaction of a lesson that finally clicks, or that quiet moment of connection with a colleague. These small moments? They’re acts of defiance against the absurd. Little ways of saying, “I matter. What I do matters,” even when the world seems indifferent.
Rejecting suicide doesn’t mean pretending everything’s okay. It’s not about denying pain or suffering. It’s about accepting all of it—and deciding to live anyway. It’s realizing that life isn’t about hunting for some hidden meaning, but about creating your own. Choosing to live authentically, without illusions or false hope.
Most people never actually make this choice consciously. They just keep going out of habit, or maybe because the alternative is scary. But if you really look the absurd in the eye, and decide to keep living, that’s an act of rebellion. It’s saying “yes” to life—even when life seems to shout “no.”
